primary_topics: Testimonial address at the San Beda Law Alumni Association dinner honoring several new judicial appointees, July 28, 2017
Tribute to the two new SC members: Justice Samuel R. Martires and Justice Noel G. Tijam -- both Bedans

CJP's analysis of People vs. Duterte: Justice Martires correctly dismissed the case outright for lack of probable cause -- not out of gratitude but on sound legal grounds, against the wishes of then-powerful House Speaker Nograles

The 'four Ins' of a good judge (integrity, independence, industry, intelligence) and the 'plague of the four ships' (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship) -- CJP's governing framework for judicial character
sub_topics: Ave Cruz's lifetime chairmanship of the SBLAA: humorously compared to Martial Law (enjoying 'the perks of martial rule... installed as the permanent and impeachment-proof chairman for life')
CJP as honorary Bedan: unanimously chosen in 2006 'by roaring acclamation, not by quiet balloting' at Cruz's 'skillful maneuvers in not allowing any objections or negative votes'

CJP's childhood Bedan aspiration: Mapa High School was opposite San Beda in Mendiola; was heading to San Beda to enroll but 'was intercepted when I was already in front of Far Eastern University -- Dean Jovito R. Salonga noticed me and led me into the FEU Institute of Law'

San Beda's missing Chief Justice: several bar topnotchers, eminent practitioners, SC and appellate court justices but no native CJ; two who could have been: Ave Cruz (declined Cory Aquino's SC offer in 1986 to serve as Deputy Prime Minister under Salvador Laurel -- short-lived when 1987 Constitution abolished the position) and Justice Bodgie Reyes (declined President Noynoy Aquino's personal telephone offer after Corona's removal -- would have been San Beda's first native CJ)

CJP's Ave Cruz tribute: greatest achievement is not in law, music or public service -- 'his greatest achievement is convincing Helen to become his wife more than 50 years ago'; CJP campaigned robustly for Cruz to become ALA President (attained February 2016)

Justice Samuel R. Martires: initially wanted to be a psychiatrist (no MD required to begin career); then the priesthood (Franciscan order; widowed mother discouraged him); became a lawyer; wife Cecilia; most prized possession is a rosary bought in Rome held during JBC interview; simple and humble: hopia and Skyflakes crackers; karaoke favorites: 'Babalik Ka Rin' (kundiman) and Tony Bennett's 'Who Can I Turn To'; SC term regrettably short (retires January 2, 2019 at 70); three priorities: corruption, 'perceived interference of government officials,' 'trial by publicity by media'

People vs. Duterte (April 14, 2011): written by Justice Martires with concurrence of Justices Villaruz and Quiroz; dismissed outright for lack of probable cause; then-Davao Mayor Duterte could not be held liable for demolishing a canal cover without permits that caused flooding; decided against the wishes of then-House Speaker Prospero Nograles (opposite political camp); 'showed that Justice Sammy had the guts to do what was correct and proper regardless of the wishes of ruling political gods'

Justice Noel G. Tijam: nominated by JBC four times (Oct 5, 2009; Nov 29, 2009; July 28, 2010; Dec 9, 2011); served CA 2003-2017 and RTC QC 1994-2003; finished law cum laude and salutatorian, San Beda 1971; Duterte was his batchmate; Justice Vit Aguirre was valedictorian; 'accidental' Bedan (enrollment queues too long at UE and UST; auntie with son in Benedictine community suggested San Beda); initial ambition: diplomat; found law 'more challenging and exciting'; retires January 5, 2019; credits everything to Lord Jesus Christ

Other honorees: new Sandiganbayan justices Maria Theresa Mendoza-Arcega, Bernelito Fernandez, Lorifel Pahinma; JBC members Justice Secretary Vitaliano Aguirre II, Judge Toribio Ilao, Congressman Reynaldo Umali

Four constitutional desiderata: 'proven competence, integrity, probity and independence'; CJP's four Ins: 'integrity, independence, industry and intelligence' -- 'of these four, independence is the most important'
Plague of the four ships: 'kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship -- they owe allegiance only to the Constitution and the law'

Quote from 'Leadership by Example' (1999): 'something does happen when (magistrates) don the black robes of this Court... they realize the god-like finality of their words and actions, for their decisions... are immortalized in books to be perused, criticized, damned or acclaimed many years after they have passed from this world'

stances.claim: Justice Samuel Martires' dismissal of People vs. Duterte was correct on the merits -- the Mayor cannot be held liable for demolishing a canal cover built without permits that caused flooding -- and not an act of political gratitude. More significantly, Martires decided it against the perceived wishes of then-powerful House Speaker Nograles (who belonged to the opposite political camp), demonstrating judicial courage and independence.
stances.rhetorical_move: merit-and-courage defense: the decision was right on the law AND required courage against powerful political interests -- making gratitude theory doubly implausible
stances.confidence: asserted after personally reading the full ponencia

stances.claim: Among CJP's four Ins of a good judge (integrity, independence, industry, intelligence), independence is the most important -- because it is the prerequisite for the other three to function properly. A judge who is subservient to the appointing authority cannot be honest about integrity, productive in industry, or correct in intelligence.
stances.rhetorical_move: hierarchy-of-virtues argument: independence as the master virtue that enables the other three
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's judicial philosophy, derived from his own judicial experience

stances.claim: San Beda has produced bar topnotchers, eminent practitioners, SC justices -- but has not yet produced its own Chief Justice because its two best candidates (Ave Cruz and Bodgie Reyes) both declined when the offer came. The lack of a native Bedan CJ is not a deficiency of talent but a consequence of personal choices made by two of its finest alumni.
stances.rhetorical_move: opportunity-cost argument: the missing Bedan CJ as the product of individual choices, not institutional inadequacy

notable_anecdotes: CJP intercepted en route to San Beda: 'as I was preparing to enter law school proper, I was heading towards San Beda to enroll from our small rented apartment in Cataluña Street in Sampaloc, Manila. However, I was intercepted when I was already in front of Far Eastern University. Dean Jovito R. Salonga noticed me and led me into the FEU Institute of Law.' His impossible dream of being a Bedan was fulfilled only when Ave Cruz proclaimed him an honorary member.

Ave Cruz's greatest achievement: 'his greatest achievement is not in law, or in music, or in public service. Not even in ALA. In my humble opinion, his greatest achievement is convincing Helen to become his wife more than 50 years ago.'

Justice Martires' career arc: wanted to be a psychiatrist (no MD required first); then the Franciscan priesthood (widowed mother discouraged him because she couldn't bear being away from her only child); became a lawyer; most prized possession: a rosary bought in Rome, held during his JBC interview; favorite snacks: hopia and Skyflakes crackers; karaoke: 'Babalik Ka Rin' or Tony Bennett's 'Who Can I Turn To.'

People vs. Duterte: CJP read the full ponencia personally and fully agreed with the dismissal -- not just on the merits but in its courage against then-powerful House Speaker Nograles who 'belonged to the opposite political camp.'

Justice Tijam as 'accidental Bedan': enrollment queues too long at UE and UST; enrolled at San Beda on an auntie's suggestion because her son was in the Benedictine community. His 1971 class: Duterte was his batchmate; Justice Vit Aguirre was valedictorian.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered July 28, 2017 at the San Beda Law Alumni Association testimonial dinner, this speech by CJP -- who describes being intercepted en route to San Beda enrollment by Salonga outside FEU and calls his honorary Bedan membership his 'impossible dream fulfilled' -- honors several new judicial appointees. He opens by comparing Ave Cruz's lifetime SBLAA chairmanship to Martial Law and noting that Cruz 'could have been the longest-serving Chief Justice' had he accepted Cory Aquino's SC offer in 1986 (instead choosing to serve as Deputy Prime Minister under Salvador Laurel -- a position abolished by the 1987 Constitution). Justice Bodgie Reyes similarly declined President Noynoy Aquino's personal telephone CJ offer, depriving San Beda of its first native Chief Justice. Cruz's 'greatest achievement,' however, is not in law or ALA but 'convincing Helen to become his wife more than 50 years ago.' The primary tribute goes to Justices Samuel Martires and Noel Tijam. On Martires: CJP personally read People vs. Duterte (April 14, 2011) and fully agrees with the dismissal for lack of probable cause -- the Mayor could not be held liable for demolishing a canal cover built without permits; crucially, Martires decided it against the perceived wishes of then-powerful House Speaker Nograles (opposite political camp), demonstrating that he 'had the guts to do what was correct and proper regardless of the wishes of ruling political gods.' Martires initially wanted to be a psychiatrist, then a Franciscan priest (his widowed mother discouraged him), became a lawyer; his most prized possession is a rosary from Rome; favorite snacks are hopia and Skyflakes; karaoke: 'Babalik Ka Rin' and Tony Bennett's 'Who Can I Turn To.' On Tijam: an 'accidental Bedan' (enrolled because enrollment queues were too long at UE and UST); 1971 class salutatorian (Duterte was his batchmate; Justice Vit Aguirre was valedictorian); served CA 2003-2017. CJP closes with his judicial character framework: the four Ins (integrity, independence, industry, intelligence -- independence is the most important) and the plague of the four ships (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship), and the canonical quote from 'Leadership by Example' (1999) on the 'god-like finality' of judicial decisions immortalized in books.
